title: Return Of The Repressed In Germany | NOEMA
gist: Nathan Gardels argues Germany's rising neo-Nazi parties, strongest in the former East and polling up to 44% in regional elections, are the 'return of the repressed': a suppressed need for belonging colliding with immigration influxes, foreseen by NPQ contributors three decades ago. He contends tighter immigration control is now a mainstream democratic response, not a shift to the right, and prescribes secure borders, a narrower asylum definition, skills-based admission (Canada's ~60% economic class) and active integration institutions.

insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Erosion of Germany's centrist coalitions raises political-risk premia for Europe's largest economy and the EU's policy cohesion.

insights.claim: Gardels frames Germany since WWII as an 'alias nation' that hid its identity under NATO and the European community, predicting that repressed national passions would resurface in ugly form.

insights.so_what: Suggests the German anchor of EU integration rests on suppressed rather than resolved identity, implying latent fragility in European institutions.

insights.claim: The disconnect between European elites' anti-nationalist integration project ('Nationalism means war', per Mitterrand) and a grassroots sense of lost home was set in motion in the 1990s and was compounded when Angela Merkel admitted some 900,000 Syrian refugees in 2015.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Elite-voter divergence on migration is a long-running structural driver, not a cyclical swing, so populist pressure is likely persistent.
insights.locator: The disconnect that has become so manifest

insights.claim: Gardels argues it is wrong to describe governments tightening immigration as 'moving to the right'; failure to balance host populations and newcomers has become a mainstream concern and democracies are responding as they should.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Expect continued tightening of migration policy across the political spectrum, not just from right-wing governments.

insights.claim: The tension between belonging and compassion for migrants is global, haunting Europe, the United States and developing regions from South Africa to the Bangladesh-India borderlands.

insights.so_what: Migration-driven political volatility is a cross-regional risk factor, not a European idiosyncrasy.

insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Even progressive local administrators facing integration costs drift toward restriction, foreshadowing today's cross-party consensus.

insights.so_what: Migration pressure is structurally tied to global inequality and will persist absent development gains in origin regions.

insights.claim: States must control immigration on criteria ensuring newcomers abide by local norms and contribute economically, because states are bound by the fiscal realities of bordered territories.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Frames immigration policy through fiscal sustainability, supporting skills-based and points-based regimes.

insights.claim: Without enforced border control up front, societies end up with 'mean-spirited and cruel crackdowns' after the fact, as Gardels says is happening in the U.S. and on the Mediterranean.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Lax enforcement now raises the probability of harsher, more disruptive crackdowns later — a policy-volatility risk.

insights.claim: Asylum should be redefined: it was meant for those persecuted or temporarily fleeing war, not as a path to permanent residency or a haven for mass exodus from weak states, and broad extension overwhelms the cultural, political and economic carrying capacity of states.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Signals intellectual support for narrowing asylum regimes, likely shaping EU asylum reform.
insights.quote: Extending asylum so broadly overwhelms the carrying capacity — culturally, politically and economically — of even the most compassionate states.

insights.claim: The next migration conundrum will be climate refugees displaced by floods, droughts and famines linked to warming for which the industrialized North bears most historical responsibility.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Climate-driven displacement is an emerging long-term source of migration and political stress for Northern democracies.
insights.locator: The next conundrum on this front

insights.claim: Aging Northern societies must abandon the illusion they can do without legal immigration, which means a more multicultural mix and proactive assimilation and integration policies.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Demographics make immigration economically necessary; the policy question shifts from whether to how to select and integrate.

insights.so_what: Poorly selected and integrated migration produces persistent social costs that fuel political backlash.

insights.claim: Canada integrates immigrants better than most because about 60% are admitted through the 'economic class' matched to labor needs, whereas in the U.S. two-thirds of permanent residents come via family reunification and under 20% on skills, per Harvard's Paul May.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Admission criteria drive integration outcomes; skills-based systems are the reference model for reform.
insights.quote: some 60% are admitted through the “economic class,”
insights.locator: Integration begins with the right immigration criteria.

insights.claim: For contiguous borders like U.S.-Mexico with strong lower-wage demand in agriculture, services and construction, Gardels favors a cross-border work permit system without permanent residency, with rigorously enforced labor rights.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: A guest-worker model could stabilize labor supply for agriculture, construction and services while limiting permanent settlement.

insights.claim: California's majority Latino and Asian, mostly second-generation population has integrated largely successfully because public higher education acts as a mixer; the CSU system has 470,000 students on 23 campuses, 48% Latino and 16% Asian.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Public higher education is a key integration infrastructure, supporting upward mobility of immigrant families into the middle class.

insights.claim: Gardels concludes that open societies need defined borders to sustain a common identity — each is a condition of the other.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Frames border control as a precondition for preserving openness rather than its opposite.
insights.quote: Open societies need defined borders to sustain a common sense of identity.
insights.locator: Open Societies Need Defined Borders
